title: THEY SAW GOD… AND DID NOT DIE. WHY?
paragraphs: THEY SAW GOD… AND DID NOT DIE. WHY?

Seventy Elders Stood Before the Holy One, Ate in His Presence, and Walked Away Alive. The Astonishing Mystery of Exodus 24:9–11—and What It Reveals About Jesus Christ, the Blood of the Covenant, and the Grace That Makes a Way for Sinners.
Imagine standing on a mountain where the presence of God has descended.
The ground beneath you is trembling with the memory of thunder. The mountain is wrapped in a holiness so overwhelming that even approaching it without God's permission could mean death.
You know what happened when God descended upon Sinai.
The people trembled.
The trumpet sounded.
Smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace.
And the mountain shook.
Now imagine something almost impossible.
You climb that same mountain.
You come into the presence of the living God.
You see something of His glory.
And instead of dying…
You sit down and eat.
No lightning strikes you.
No judgment consumes you.
No divine hand destroys you.
You are still breathing.
Still alive.
Still sitting in the presence of the One whose holiness makes the heavens tremble.
That is not a fictional scene.
That is Exodus 24.

And buried inside these three extraordinary verses is a truth about God's holiness, covenant mercy, and the coming of Jesus Christ that could completely change how you understand what it means to approach God.
But there is one detail most people rush past.
One sentence.
Just a few words.
And those words hold the key to the entire encounter.
“Also they saw God, and did eat and drink.” — Exodus 24:11, KJV
Read that again.
They saw God.
And they ate.
And they drank.
How could sinful human beings survive such an encounter?
And why does the answer lead us all the way to the cross of Jesus Christ?
Because this was never simply a story about men climbing a mountain.
It was a revelation of what happens when a holy God graciously makes a way for human beings to draw near.
And perhaps, by the time you finish reading, you will realize something about your own life.
The greatest miracle is not that these men stood before God and survived.
It is that God has made a way for people like us to come near to Him at all.
The story begins with names.
Moses.
Aaron.
Nadab.
Abihu.
And seventy of the elders of Israel.
Exodus 24:9–10 tells us:

“Then went up Moses, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel: And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.” (KJV)
Stop there.
The Hebrew text uses a remarkable expression.
וַיִּרְאוּ אֵת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayir'u et Elohei Yisra'el.
“And they saw the God of Israel.”
The verb וַיִּרְאוּ (vayir'u) comes from ראה (ra'ah), meaning “to see.”
The biblical writer is not merely saying that they felt something spiritual or had a vague religious impression.
He deliberately describes a real encounter in which God made Himself perceptible to them.
But notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say they comprehended God's infinite essence.
It does not say they saw the full, unveiled glory of His being.
It does not even give us a description of God's face.
Instead, the passage directs our attention downward.
To what appeared beneath His feet.
Something resembling sapphire pavement.
Something as clear as the heavens themselves.
The description is breathtaking.
But it is also restrained.
It communicates the majesty of God's presence without pretending that the infinite Creator can be contained within a human description.
And this distinction matters.
Because later, in Exodus 33:20, God tells Moses:
“Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.” (KJV)
So which is it?
Did Moses see God?
Or can no one see God and live?
Both passages are true. The difference is between seeing a manifestation God graciously permits and beholding the fullness of His unveiled glory.
God is not contradicting Himself.
He is revealing the difference between His infinite holiness and the limited ways He chooses to make Himself known to human beings.
The elders truly encountered God.
But they did not exhaustively behold His divine essence.
They saw what God allowed them to see.
They approached because God permitted them to approach.
And they lived because God graciously preserved them.
That is the first truth we must understand.
God's holiness had not become less dangerous. God had mercifully made their approach possible.
And if you read the chapter carefully, you discover something astonishing.
Before they ever climbed the mountain…
There was blood.
Exodus 24 does not begin with a meal.
It begins with a covenant.
Moses communicates the words of the LORD to the people. The people promise obedience. Sacrifices are offered. Blood is collected.
Then Moses takes the blood and sprinkles it upon the people, declaring:
“Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you concerning all these words.” (Exodus 24:8, KJV)
Only after this covenant ceremony does the account describe Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders ascending.
Do you see the order?
The covenant is ratified with blood.
Then the representatives of Israel are granted this extraordinary encounter.
We must be careful here.

The text does not explicitly say that the blood functioned as a magical shield against God's presence. Nor should we imagine that animal sacrifices possessed power independent of God's gracious covenant.
But the sequence is unmistakable.
The mountain encounter takes place within a covenant relationship established by God and solemnly ratified through sacrificial blood.
And this is where the story begins to point forward.
Because centuries later, another covenant would be announced.
Another sacrifice would be offered.
And another meal would reveal something extraordinary about God's desire to dwell with His people.
But this time, the sacrifice would not be a bull upon an altar.
It would be the Son of God upon a cross.
Before we reach Calvary, however, we must return to one of the most haunting sentences in the entire chapter.
Exodus 24:11 says:
“And upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: also they saw God, and did eat and drink.” (KJV)
There it is.
The detail that changes everything.
“He laid not his hand.”
In Hebrew:
לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ
Lo shalach yado.
Literally, “He did not stretch out His hand.”
In this context, the expression communicates that God did not extend His hand against these men in judgment.
Think about that.
The narrator deliberately tells us that God did not strike them.
Why mention it?
Because standing before the Holy One was not something sinful human beings could casually presume upon.
The absence of judgment was worth recording.
Their survival was not ordinary.
It was mercy.
The men were alive in God's presence because God chose not to destroy them.
And that should make every one of us think.
We live in a generation that sometimes speaks about God as though He were merely a comforting idea.
Someone to call when life becomes difficult.
Someone expected to approve whatever we desire.
Someone whose holiness can be ignored as long as we occasionally acknowledge His existence.
But the God of Exodus is not a harmless religious accessory.
He is the Creator.
The Judge of all the earth.
The One who is perfectly righteous.
The One before whom sin cannot be treated as insignificant.
And yet…
He is also the God who invites people into covenant fellowship.
The God who reveals Himself.
The God who provides a way of approach.
The God whose mercy is as real as His holiness.
That is why this passage should not merely make us curious.
It should make us humble.
Because if we are honest, many of us have spent years wanting the comfort of God's presence while resisting the authority of His Word.
We want His peace.
But not always His correction.
We want His blessings.
But not always His commands.
We want forgiveness.
But sometimes we keep making room for the very sins from which Christ calls us to turn.
And perhaps the hardest truth is this:
We can become so familiar with the language of grace that we forget how astonishing grace actually is.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward those who cannot save themselves.
And the cross shows us just how seriously God takes both sin and salvation.
Now look again at the elders.
They saw God.
And they ate and drank.
Why a meal?
Why not simply bow down and leave?
Because in the ancient biblical world, shared meals could express fellowship, peace, and covenant relationship.
Exodus 24 does not provide a menu or explicitly identify every aspect of the meal's symbolism.
But its setting is unmistakably covenantal.
After the blood of the covenant, these representatives of Israel eat and drink in God's presence.
It is a remarkable picture of fellowship granted by divine mercy.
The God who descended upon Sinai in terrifying holiness now allows these men to experience communion in His presence.
Not because they have become divine.
Not because they have earned the right to stand before Him.
But because He has graciously welcomed them within His covenant.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Some of you know what it feels like to believe God is holy but struggle to believe He would welcome someone with your history.
You remember what you did.
The secret compromises.
The promises you made and broke.
The prayer you stopped praying because you felt ashamed to ask again.
The season when you looked faithful in public but were quietly falling apart in private.
You know how to smile in church.
You know how to say, “I'm blessed.”
You know how to encourage someone else.
But there are nights when the room becomes quiet and the memories come back.
And you wonder…
If God knew everything about me, would He still want me near Him?
Here is the truth.
He already knows.
Every hidden thought.
Every buried failure.
Every wound.
Every act of disobedience.
Every excuse.
Every moment of genuine repentance.
And the Gospel does not tell you that God welcomes sinners because He has overlooked their sin.
It tells you that Jesus Christ came to save sinners through His death and resurrection.
That is far greater than pretending our failures never happened.
It means our sins can be forgiven through the One who bore sin's judgment.
It means shame does not have to become our permanent identity.
It means the person who turns to Christ in repentance and faith does not have to remain enslaved to the past.
And this is why Exodus 24 becomes even more beautiful when read in the light of the New Testament.
On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus sat at a table with His disciples.
He took the cup.
And according to Matthew 26:28, He said:
“For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.” (KJV)
The Greek reads:
τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης
Touto gar estin to haima mou tēs diathēkēs.
“For this is my blood of the covenant…”
The word διαθήκη (diathēkē) means “covenant” in this biblical context.
The connection with Exodus 24 is profound.
At Sinai, Moses declared the blood of the covenant.
At the Last Supper, Jesus identified His own blood with the covenant.
The Gospels present Jesus' death as the sacrifice through which the promised new covenant is established.
And Hebrews makes the connection between covenant, blood, and Christ's saving work unmistakable.
Hebrews 9:15 calls Jesus the mediator of the new covenant.
Hebrews 9:22 emphasizes the importance of blood in the sacrificial system's treatment of purification and forgiveness.
Hebrews 10:19–22 announces that believers have confidence to enter God's holy presence through the blood of Jesus.
Do not miss the difference.
At Sinai, the elders were granted an extraordinary encounter under the old covenant.
In Christ, believers receive access to God through the perfect and sufficient sacrifice of the new covenant Mediator.
We should not claim that Exodus 24 explicitly describes the Last Supper or that every detail is a direct prediction of it.
But the canonical connection is real.
The blood of the covenant at Sinai prepares us to understand the greater covenant secured by the blood of Jesus Christ.
And the fellowship meal on the mountain helps us appreciate the astonishing grace of being welcomed into communion with God.
Now consider something else.
The elders did not climb the mountain because they were morally flawless.
And Scripture later makes that painfully clear.
Two of the men named in this extraordinary encounter were Nadab and Abihu.
The sons of Aaron.
Men who had witnessed something of God's glory.
Men who had been present at this covenantal meal.
And yet, in Leviticus 10, Nadab and Abihu later offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.
Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them.
They died.
Let that sink in.
Two men who once ate in God's presence later died under His judgment.
That detail should silence the dangerous assumption that a powerful spiritual experience automatically guarantees lifelong faithfulness.
You can witness something extraordinary and still need to obey God.
You can have a moving encounter and still be accountable for what you do afterward.
You can know the language of worship and still allow disobedience into your heart.
An unforgettable moment with God is not a substitute for an obedient walk with God.
And this is not written to make tenderhearted believers despair.
It is a warning against presumption.
God's grace should lead us toward reverence, gratitude, repentance, and faithfulness—not careless confidence that our choices no longer matter.
Maybe you remember a season when your faith was alive.
You prayed with tears.
You opened your Bible with hunger.
You worshiped without worrying who was watching.
You wanted nothing more than to honor Jesus.
But somewhere along the way, your heart became distracted.
A compromise seemed small.
A secret habit became familiar.
A bitterness remained unresolved.
A prayer life slowly disappeared.
And now you are living on the memory of a fire that no longer seems to burn the way it once did.
Please hear this.
You do not need to manufacture another emotional experience to impress God.
You need to return to Christ.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what needs to be abandoned.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And begin walking in obedience again.
First John 1:9 tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
There is hope for the repentant.
There is mercy for the broken.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
And the same Gospel that calls you out of sin also assures you that you do not have to save yourself.
Christ has done what you could never do.
But perhaps you are still troubled by the original question.
How could the elders see God when Exodus 33 says no one can see His face and live?
The New Testament gives us another essential piece of the answer.
John 1:18 declares:
“No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” (KJV)
John's Gospel emphasizes that God is made known through His Son.
The Greek verb translated “declared” is ἐξηγήσατο (exēgēsato), from a verb meaning to explain, recount, or make known.
Jesus Christ uniquely reveals the Father.
This does not mean that Exodus 24 was imaginary.
Nor does it require us to insist that the elders saw God's essence.
It means that God's self-revelation reaches its supreme clarity in Jesus Christ.

Some Christian interpreters understand Old Testament appearances of God as manifestations of the preincarnate Son. Others interpret Exodus 24 more cautiously as a divinely granted vision or manifestation without identifying the visible form specifically as the Son.
Exodus 24 itself does not explicitly settle that question.
What Scripture does make clear is that Jesus Christ is the definitive revelation of God.
Colossians 1:15 calls Him “the image of the invisible God.”
And Hebrews 1:3 describes Him as “the express image of his person” in the KJV.
So if you want to know what God's saving mercy looks like…
Look to Jesus.
If you want to know whether God takes sin seriously…
Look to the cross.
If you want to know whether forgiveness is possible…
Look to the risen Savior.
And if you want to know whether a broken sinner can be welcomed into fellowship with God…
Listen to what the Gospel announces.
Romans 5:1–2 says:

“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God.” (KJV)
Peace with God.
Not because we have become sinless through our own efforts.
Not because our religious performance has earned divine approval.
But through our Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
The holy God who cannot compromise His righteousness has provided salvation through His Son.
Jesus lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And all who truly turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and new life.
This is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is an invitation to leave rebellion behind.
And now the mountain of Exodus 24 begins to look different.
Because the most astonishing part of the story is no longer simply that the elders survived.
It is that their encounter belongs to a much larger biblical story.
A story that moves from Sinai to Calvary.
From covenant blood to the blood of Christ.
From a mountain where selected representatives were permitted to approach…
To a Savior through whom believers are invited to draw near to God.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” (KJV)
Notice the invitation.
Come boldly.
Not arrogantly.
Not carelessly.
Not pretending sin is harmless.
But confidently, because Jesus is our great High Priest.
The confidence belongs to those who trust in Him.
The mercy comes from God.
The access is secured by Christ.
And perhaps that is what your soul has been starving for.
Not another religious performance.
Not another week of pretending you have everything together.
Not another attempt to hide your wounds behind a polished Christian image.
But genuine fellowship with the living God.
The kind of fellowship that changes how you live when nobody is watching.
The kind that makes you honest about sin without leaving you trapped in condemnation.
The kind that teaches you to love what Christ loves and turn away from what grieves Him.
The kind that reminds you that the Christian life is not merely about surviving judgment.
It is about knowing the God who saves.
Think about the elders one final time.
They were on a mountain.
Before them was a manifestation of divine glory.
Beneath God's feet was something like sapphire, clear as the heavens.
And the Bible tells us that He did not stretch out His hand against them.
They ate.
They drank.
They lived.
Now imagine what it means that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, willingly gave His life so that sinners could be reconciled to the Father.
The elders did not deserve to control God's presence.
Neither do we.
They depended upon divine mercy.
So do we.
But we have been given something they could only anticipate within the unfolding history of redemption.
We have the revelation of Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
We know the name of the Savior.
We have heard the announcement of the new covenant.
We have been told that forgiveness is available through Him.
And that changes everything.
The question is no longer merely, “How did Moses and the elders survive seeing God?”
The question becomes deeply personal.
“What will I do with the grace God has offered me through Jesus Christ?”
Will I keep hiding?
Will I keep postponing repentance?
Will I continue treating God's mercy as though it were ordinary?
Or will I finally surrender?
Not because I can earn His love.
But because His love has been revealed so powerfully in Jesus Christ.
If you have wandered, come back to Him.
If you are carrying secret sin, bring it into the light.
If you are exhausted from trying to appear spiritually strong, stop pretending and begin praying honestly.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ as your Savior, do not confuse admiration for Christianity with saving faith in Christ.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
There is no greater rescue than the salvation He provides.
And there is no greater privilege than being reconciled to God.
Perhaps this article has reminded you of someone.
A brother who no longer attends church.
A daughter who thinks she has gone too far.
A friend who believes their past makes them unacceptable to God.
A believer who has quietly drifted away.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus had to die.
Not simply to increase its reach.
But because someone scrolling through their feed tonight may be asking a question they have never dared to say out loud:
“Could God still forgive someone like me?”
A single shared message of Scripture cannot save anyone by itself. Salvation belongs to the Lord.
But God can use His Word, shared faithfully, to point someone toward the Savior.
And I want to invite you to do something more than simply react to what you have read.
Have you ever felt unworthy to approach God because of something in your past?
Have you ever confused a powerful spiritual experience with a faithful daily walk?
Have you ever discovered that God's grace was greater than the shame you were carrying?
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers.
Sometimes a simple testimony is enough to encourage someone who thought they were fighting alone.
Return to Exodus 24.
Read the entire chapter.
Compare it with Exodus 33, Matthew 26, John 1, and Hebrews 9–10.
Do not simply take my words as the final authority.
Let Scripture test what you have read.
Because the goal of Gospel Warrior is not to make you dependent upon an article.
It is to help you become more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ and His Word.
That is why I also want to speak openly about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Every article, biblical teaching, devotional, and discipleship resource represents an opportunity to encourage believers, reach searching hearts, and proclaim the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And that mission requires time, dedication, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe that biblical truth should continue reaching others.
It does not purchase blessings, forgiveness, spiritual protection, or a closer relationship with Christ.
Those things cannot be bought.
Scripture teaches us that giving should be willing and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to glorify Christ by helping biblical teaching reach more people.
These are simply thank-you benefits, not spiritual rewards.
The greater purpose is the mission.
To keep pointing people toward Jesus.
To help believers grow in biblical understanding.
To encourage repentance, restoration, and faithful discipleship.
And to make sound Christian resources more accessible.
Because the Word of God is not a commodity to be withheld from people who cannot afford to give.
You can still pray.
You can still share biblical teachings.
You can still help bring the message of Jesus Christ to someone who desperately needs hope.
It is about the Savior.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who transforms lives through His grace.
The One who alone deserves the glory.
And now, before you leave this story, remember the mountain one last time.
Seventy elders.
Moses.
Aaron.
Nadab.
Abihu.
The God of Israel.
The sapphire-like pavement.
The blood of the covenant.
The extraordinary meal.
And that unforgettable declaration:
“Upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand.”
They lived because God mercifully permitted them to remain in His presence.
And today, the Gospel announces that through Jesus Christ, sinners who repent and believe may be reconciled to that same holy God.
Not because holiness has changed.
Not because sin no longer matters.
Not because we have become worthy through our own efforts.
But because Jesus Christ is the sufficient Savior.
The cross does not make God's holiness disappear.
It reveals both His righteousness and His saving love.
The resurrection declares the victory of the One who died for our sins.
And the invitation remains.
Come to Christ.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in His truth.
Do not spend your entire life standing at a distance from the grace God has made known in His Son.
Because the greatest wonder of Exodus 24 is not simply that sinful men stood before a holy God and lived.
It is that their encounter helps prepare us to understand the greater mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
They stood on a mountain and lived to tell of God's mercy. Jesus died on a hill and rose again so that those who trust in Him could live forever in God's presence.
